perspective:
Harold Padilla’s available information:

- He knows he is Harold Padilla, a project manager. He knows Arthur as a friend/professional contact he relies on for advice and support.
- He felt frustrated and anxious about the project’s progress and believed his team was not performing well due to lack of motivation.
- He arranged and attended a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur. He told Arthur his team seemed unmotivated and that it was affecting progress. He heard Arthur advise understanding each team member’s individual motivations and having one-on-one conversations. He decided to try this and felt more hopeful.
- He felt hopeful and relieved, believed Arthur’s advice would help, and proposed one-on-one chats to his team about what motivates them. He heard one team member say it could be helpful and another say they were open to it. He said he would schedule time with each of them.
- He later observed that the team still was not responding well. He felt disappointed and worried, and told Arthur that the suggestions had not worked. He heard Arthur suggest deeper issues, such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and the need to dig deeper. He decided to hold another round of one-on-one meetings.
- In those meetings, he asked team members to share concerns. He heard one team member report tension among some team members that was affecting work, and another report feeling overwhelmed and stressed by the workload. He said he would look into resolving conflicts and consider redistributing tasks, and that their well-being mattered.
- He felt optimistic and empowered, believed addressing individual concerns would improve performance, and announced regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He heard team members support the idea. He said their input and well-being were crucial to the project’s success.

He does not have access to hidden thoughts, private motives, or narrator-only information about Arthur or the team beyond what he observed or was told in these interactions.
